To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a patient with Kartageners' syndrome had immotile ciliary and flagellar dynein arms in his somatic cells, but normal spermatozoal dynein arms, indicating that the gene for the protein that functions in spermatozoa is different than that for the protein that normally functions in cilia and flagellum.
the Kartagener's patient had immotile respiratory and efferent duct cilia, but motile spermatozoa with normal ultrastructure.
Kartagener's patients have cilia with no dynein arms and that spermatozoa from Kartagener patients have normal ultrastructure including dynein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of gene expression during the differentiation of male germ cells.
the regulation of gene expression in the male germ line and its relationship to male infertility.
the regulation of gene expression during spermatogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Kartagener's patient described in this study has an autosomal recessive gene that codes for a protein essential to the assembly and maintenance of dynein arms on cilia and flagellum in somatic tissues, but not in the testis.
the cilia of the patient described here lack dynein arms because the gene coding for the protein responsible for their synthesis has been deleted or is nonfunctional.

the patient with Kartagner's syndrome described in this paper has two different genes coding for proteins with analogous functions, one gene being expressed in somatic tissue, the other in the germ tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a mutation in a single gene may result in a spectrum of phenotypes ranging from a complete lack of cilia and flagellar motility to a normal complement of motile spermatozoa.
a mutation in a single gene may have a differential effect in different cell types, depending on the genetic background of the cell.
the patient with Kartageneer's syndrome has a mutation in the gene for the ciliary dynein arm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the testis is a unique organ with respect to the expression of genes that code for proteins with analogous functions in the somatic and germ cells.
there are genes expressed in the male germ cells that may be differentially regulated from those genes in somatic cells.
the testis is a very complex organ that is not completely understood.
